html:
Land reform in Taiwan was carried out by the Nationalist government in three steps between 1949 and 1953. Rents were cut to 37.5 per cent of the harvest, public land was sold to farmers, and the Land to the Tiller Act of 1953 made landlords sell their extra land to their tenants.

The Nationalists, who had lost China partly by failing to reform land, now did so on an island where they owned none of it. Landlords were paid partly in shares of state companies, which moved their wealth into industry.

Farm incomes and harvests rose, and the countryside became a market for local factories. Economists often cite it, with the reforms in South Korea and Japan, as a base of the East Asian boom that later produced Hsinchu and TSMC. It also took the rural elite's power and helped the newly arrived government hold the island.
